title: Manufacturing and cross-industry solution patterns
summary: Frame a use case from operational source to responsible human action: fix grain, event identity, units, timestamps and asset hierarchies, apply them to quality, traceability, engineering, maintenance, demand, scheduling and documents, transfer them across industries, and write an honest brief.
objectives: Draw a use case's chain from operational source through governed data and a decision to the responsible person, and write its metric contract at a declared grain.
Choose event identity, unit, timestamp and effective-dated hierarchy rules for plant data, and apply them to quality, traceability, engineering, maintenance, demand, scheduling and document patterns.
Transfer a pattern to retail, financial services or healthcare and evaluate candidate use cases on evidence, including a 'not enough evidence yet' verdict.

questions.prompt: Cinderline's two plants both report 'first-pass yield'. Plant A counts a unit as passing when it passes its final inspection; plant B counts only units passing the first inspection without rework. What must the shared metric contract fix first?

options.text: The dashboard refresh schedule for both plants.
options.rationale: Refreshing more often republishes two different definitions faster; it does not make them comparable.

options.text: The numerator: units passing the first inspection without rework, over units entering the operation.
options.rationale: Correct: plant A is publishing final yield under the FPY name, so the definition itself must be fixed before any comparison.

options.text: An average of the two plants' figures as the group number.
options.rationale: Averaging combines two different metrics and weights plants equally regardless of volume.

options.text: Colour thresholds so both plants show green above 95%.
options.rationale: Thresholds are cosmetic and hide that plant A's number counts reworked units as passes.

questions.prompt: A grocery retailer transfers Cinderline's event-identity pattern to point-of-sale data. Which identity keeps a return from appearing as an unlinked negative sale?

options.rationale: Two identical items sold in the same second collide, and nothing links the return to the sale it reverses.
Store systems can reuse transaction numbers, the same collision as two MES systems sharing INS-4471.

options.text: Store, transaction id and line number, with the return carrying the original sale's reference.
options.rationale: Correct: the identity is unique across stores and the reference lets the return offset its original line.

options.text: A hash of each row's payload.
options.rationale: A hash detects resends of identical rows but cannot link a return to the sale it reverses.

questions.prompt: Spindle failure prediction has 6 labelled failures across 14 spindles in two years, failure codes only since 2025 and sensors moved without dates. Which conclusion belongs in the brief?

options.text: Proceed: a first model already scores 99% accuracy.
options.rationale: With six positives, predicting that nothing fails is about 99% accurate too, so accuracy says nothing here.
The evidence does not support a permanent no either; coded failures and dated mounts could make it viable.

options.text: Proceed with a vendor's pre-trained model to avoid the label problem.
options.rationale: A pre-trained model still has to be evaluated on Cinderline's failures, which are the missing evidence.

options.text: Not enough evidence yet: code failures, date sensor mounts, and review the verdict in six months.
options.rationale: Correct: it states what is missing, how it will be collected and when the decision will be revisited.

cards.prompt: What four links must a manufacturing use case have before it can be evaluated?
cards.answer: An operational source, governed data with a declared grain and owner, a decision with a fixed action set, and a named person whose action and outcome are recorded.
cards.explanation: The last link produces the only evidence of value. A score that reaches a dashboard with no owner changes nothing and leaves no outcome rows, so no one can ever say whether the use case worked or should be retired.

cards.prompt: Three lots scrap 10 of 1,000, 20 of 200 and 8 of 800. Why do both 4.0% and 1.9% circulate?
cards.answer: 4.0% is the unweighted mean of the lot rates; 1.9% is the pooled rate, 38 scrapped over 2,000 started, which the contract should name.
cards.explanation: Averaging ratios gives the small 10% lot the same weight as the 1,000-unit lot. Neither sum is wrong arithmetic, but only a written metric contract decides which one is published as scrap rate and prevents two numbers under one name.

cards.prompt: Why is inspection_id alone a poor event identity when two plants' MES systems feed one table?
cards.answer: Two systems can issue the same number, so keying on it merges different inspections and lets one plant's result overwrite another's.
cards.explanation: In the example, plant B's INS-4471 FAIL replaces plant A's INS-4471 PASS when rows are deduplicated on inspection_id. Adding the source system and a revision keeps collisions apart, collapses genuine resends and keeps corrections as history.

cards.prompt: What should be stored for a sensor reading so the autumn clock change cannot merge two readings?
cards.answer: The UTC instant of the event, the site's time zone, the raw device time and the receive time, with local time derived rather than used as a key.
cards.explanation: Local 01:30 occurs twice on the night clocks go back. As instants the two readings are an hour apart; as local text they are identical, so a deduplication or join on local time silently drops or merges one of them.

cards.prompt: Sensor S-118 moved from DC-07 to DC-09 on 15 June. How should a reading from 10 June find its machine?
cards.answer: Join on sensor_id where the reading time falls inside a mount row's valid-from and valid-to period, which returns DC-07.
cards.explanation: A table holding only the current parent files the 10 June reading under DC-09 and corrupts DC-09's history. Effective-dated mount rows keep each reading with the machine that held the sensor at the time; a test should confirm every reading joins exactly one mount.

cards.prompt: Of 500 castings, 440 pass first time, 45 after rework and 15 are scrapped. What do final yield and first-pass yield each show?
cards.answer: Final yield, 97.0%, shows what ships; first-pass yield, 88.0%, shows how much passes without rework, exposing a 9.0% rework load.
cards.explanation: Final yield hides rework because reworked units eventually pass. First-pass yield divides first-time passes by all units entering the operation, so it reveals the line time and cost spent on rework that the healthier-looking figure absorbs.

cards.prompt: Why does mixed consumption widen a backward trace from a finished lot?
cards.answer: A lot that consumed several input lots has several parents, so where-from must follow every one of them, reaching more suppliers' lots.
cards.explanation: Assembly lot A-802 consumed casting lots C-3302 and C-3303, which came from different ingot lots. A complaint on A-802 therefore implicates both AL-5521 and AL-5522, whereas a lot with a single input would lead to one supplier lot.

cards.prompt: Serial 1063 should carry seal S-12 by BOM effectivity but consumed S-10. What should the analysis do?
cards.answer: Report the deviation with both records to the engineering owner, and trace the seal actually consumed; never edit either record so they agree.
cards.explanation: The BOM revision says what should be built and the genealogy says what was. The difference may be an approved substitution or an error, which only engineering can decide; overwriting either record destroys the evidence needed to decide it.

cards.prompt: Why must a maintenance model's prediction horizon exceed the planner's parts lead time?
cards.answer: Because a warning that arrives with less notice than it takes to get parts and plan work cannot change what happens.
cards.explanation: If bearings take 7 days to arrive, a model that flags a failure 3 days ahead can be accurate and still useless. The horizon starts at the prediction time and must leave room for the planner's lead time before the failure it predicts.

cards.prompt: What does a stock-out do to a week of shipment history used for demand forecasting?
cards.answer: It censors that week: shipments are only a lower bound on demand, so the week must be flagged before training or evaluation.
cards.explanation: A forecast trained on shipments during stock-outs learns that demand was lower than it was, and the error concentrates in exactly the fast movers that ran out. Flagging, excluding or modelling censored periods removes that systematic low bias.

cards.prompt: An order's alloy arrives a day after its due-date slot. What should the scheduling tool and the planner each do?
cards.answer: The tool produces a feasible schedule that places the order after the alloy arrives; the planner chooses and records how to handle the resulting lateness.
cards.explanation: No sequence removes lateness that a material constraint forces. The tool's job is feasibility and minimal disruption; expediting the alloy, splitting the order or notifying the customer is a business trade-off for the accountable planner, recorded with the snapshot used.

cards.prompt: Which metadata must each indexed chunk of a work instruction carry before an assistant may cite it?
cards.answer: Document id, revision, status, effective date, site and access group, copied from the controlled document system at indexing time.
cards.explanation: Without status and effective date, ranking prefers whichever wording matches the question, often a superseded revision. Filtering on this metadata before ranking, and citing the revision, lets the technician check the controlled copy that remains the authority.

cards.prompt: When moving the lot-genealogy pattern to a grocery retailer, what replaces the ingot-to-assembly edges?
cards.answer: Supplier lot to distribution centre receipt to store receipt, so a supplier recall notice can be scoped to the stores and days that received the lot.
cards.explanation: The pattern is the same walk over consumption or receipt edges, and the data problem is the same: completeness of lot capture. The event identity, grain, clock and the owners who decide what to do with the scope are the retailer's own.

cards.prompt: What must a 'not enough evidence yet' verdict contain to be useful rather than a polite no?
cards.answer: The evidence that exists, the evidence that is missing, how and by whom it will be collected, and when the verdict will be reviewed.
cards.explanation: Stated this way the verdict becomes a plan: the spindle case lists six labelled failures, uncoded history and undated sensor mounts, then names coding, mount reconstruction and a six-month review. Without those parts it cannot be acted on or revisited.
